content: Thumb-in-palm deformity is a condition observed in patients with spastic cerebral palsy that significantly impairs thumb function, thereby limiting overall hand utility. This deformity poses challenges in performing daily activities and affects the quality of life. Despite the variety of surgical techniques described in the literature, there is no established consensus on the optimal surgical approach for managing this condition. The primary objectives of this review were to evaluate the effectiveness of surgical interventions for thumb-in-palm deformity in patients with spastic cerebral palsy, to examine the criteria used to select patients for surgery, and to assess the outcome measures employed in these studies. To achieve this, studies were identified through comprehensive searches of multiple electronic databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and CINAHL, covering publications up to December 2004. Reference lists of relevant studies were also reviewed to identify additional sources. Eligible studies were required to meet specific criteria: they had to be randomized clinical trials, controlled clinical trials, or prospective studies comparing preoperative and postoperative outcomes. The studies needed to focus on patients with thumb-in-palm deformity due to spastic cerebral palsy, with no age restrictions. They also had to evaluate surgical interventions targeting the thumb, follow patients for at least six months, and report outcomes such as success rates, functional improvement, range of motion, grasp and release, pinch grip, complications, and quality of life. Two authors independently assessed the quality of the studies using a scoring system. However, due to the poor design and heterogeneity of the studies, meta-analysis was not feasible. Instead, a descriptive summary of the findings was compiled. Raw data from the studies were not obtained for re-analysis. A total of 14 prospective studies were initially identified, but only nine met the inclusion criteria. These nine studies involved 234 patients, with ages at the time of surgery ranging from 4 to 48 years (median age approximately 11 years). The surgical interventions described in these studies aimed to stabilize the first metacarpophalangeal joint, weaken the spastic thumb adductors, and enhance thumb abduction and extension. A total of 24 different surgical techniques or combinations of techniques were reported. The primary outcome measure across all studies was whether the thumb remained out of the palm during follow-up. Additional outcome measures varied widely among studies, reflecting a lack of standardization in assessment methods. Most of the assessment tools used were not validated, making it difficult to compare results across studies. There was also no consensus on the criteria for selecting patients for surgery. The studies generally reported satisfactory outcomes from surgical treatment, with improvements in hand function, hygiene, appearance, and quality of life. However, due to the variability in surgical techniques and the use of co-interventions, it was not possible to determine the effectiveness of any specific surgical procedure. The authors concluded that the poor methodological quality of the included studies prevents a reliable assessment of the role of surgery in managing thumb-in-palm deformity. There is a clear need for well-designed randomized clinical trials or controlled clinical trials to evaluate the effectiveness of surgical interventions. Future research should focus on developing a validated classification system to guide patient selection and determine the type and extent of cerebral palsy-related hand deformities. Additionally, factors such as age, intelligence, and voluntary muscle control should be investigated to better understand their influence on surgical outcomes. Researchers should aim to evaluate specific surgical techniques or groups of interventions to identify those that provide the greatest functional improvement.
